name: sshuttle
desc: Proxy server that works as a poor man's VPN
why: Tunnels whole subnets over SSH using packet capture tricks, a neat door into how transparent proxying and routing actually work.

brief.what_it_is: sshuttle is a command-line proxy that tunnels network traffic over an SSH connection, acting as a lightweight stand-in for a VPN. You point it at a remote SSH host and at the subnets you want to reach, and it forwards every port on those networks, not just ports you name in advance. Clients see the real IP addresses of remote hosts rather than localhost port mappings. The README says it runs on Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, and Windows (experimental).
brief.why_it_exists: The README targets people who can reach a remote network over SSH but have no usable VPN there, may lack admin rights on that network, and find OpenSSH port forwarding too slow or cumbersome for many hosts. It also argues that OpenSSH's PermitTunnel is disabled by default and does TCP-over-TCP, which performs badly.
brief.how_it_works: The how-it-works page says sshuttle is 'not exactly a VPN, and not exactly port forwarding.' It tracks every connection instead of forwarding packets statelessly: it reassembles the TCP stream locally, multiplexes it statefully over one SSH session, and splits it back into packets at the far end. The stated result is data-over-TCP rather than TCP-over-TCP, which avoids the performance collapse the docs attribute to tunnelling raw packets over a reliable transport.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install: packages exist for Ubuntu, Debian, Arch, Fedora, openSUSE, Gentoo, NixOS, FreeBSD (ports or pkg), OpenBSD, MacPorts, and Nix (nix-shell -p sshuttle). Python installs go through PyPI or a git clone with pip. Windows is listed as 'pip install sshuttle' with a separate experimental Windows page. I did not fetch the Requirements or Usage pages, so client privileges, remote-side requirements, and first-run steps are unverified.
brief.standout: Instead of tunnelling packets through SSH, which the author says causes TCP-over-TCP meltdown, it keeps per-connection state, so the tunnel carries plain data and the inner TCP sessions behave normally. The README also says the author knows of no other program that covers this exact combination of client OS, ssh-only access, no admin on the remote side, and no VPN. That claim is hedged with 'as far as I know'.
brief.status: Appears maintained, but I could not confirm dates. The stable docs are for version 2.0.0, and the README links both stable and latest documentation and a write-up on running it as a service. I saw no release date or commit date.
brief.caveats: Windows support is marked experimental in the README. The README says nothing about licensing, which I did not check. The README points to a Medium post for running it as a service, which is third-party guidance rather than project documentation. Its approach of tracking connections is presented as the reason it avoids TCP-over-TCP, not as a limit, but I did not read the Requirements, Usage, or TPROXY pages, so platform limits beyond those listed are unknown.
quotes: sshuttle: where transparent proxy meets VPN meets ssh
sshuttle is not exactly a VPN, and not exactly port forwarding.  It's kind of both, and kind of neither.
It's just data-over-TCP, which is safe.

judge.reason: Its stateful TCP-stream tunneling over SSH makes transparent access to remote subnets possible without a conventional VPN, revealing an unusual networking design.

entry.title: sshuttle
entry.tldr: Tunnels whole subnets over a plain SSH connection, so you reach a remote network by its real addresses without a VPN or admin rights.
entry.deeper_look:
sshuttle is a command-line proxy that sends your network traffic through an SSH connection. You give it a remote SSH host and the subnets you want to reach, and it forwards every port on those networks, not only the ones you named in advance. Programs on your machine see the remote hosts' real IP addresses, not a pile of localhost port mappings.

The README aims it at a specific situation: you can SSH into a remote network, there is no usable VPN, you may lack admin rights there, and OpenSSH port forwarding is too slow or fiddly for many hosts. It also points out that OpenSSH's PermitTunnel is off by default and carries TCP over TCP, which performs badly.

The idea underneath is the interesting part. The how-it-works page says sshuttle is "not exactly a VPN, and not exactly port forwarding." It tracks every connection: it reassembles the TCP stream locally, multiplexes it statefully over one SSH session, and splits it back into packets at the far end. In the project's words, "It's just data-over-TCP, which is safe." Reading that page is a short way into how transparent proxying and TCP behaviour work.
entry.install:
brew install sshuttle

Needs a host you can reach over SSH. I did not verify the client privileges or remote-side requirements, so check the Requirements page in the docs before the first run.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the options, including how to name the remote host and the subnets to route through it.

entry.whats_unique: It keeps per-connection state instead of tunnelling raw packets, which avoids TCP-over-TCP. The README also says it knows of no other program that fits this combination of client OS, ssh-only access, no remote admin rights and no VPN.
entry.caveats: Windows support is marked experimental, and I could not confirm recent release dates, though the project appears maintained.
